cardio-wb-cardio1-q10.answer:
The most common cause of right-sided heart failure is left-sided heart failure: raised left-sided filling pressures are transmitted back through the pulmonary veins, raise pulmonary artery pressure, and overload the right ventricle.

When the right heart fails from lung disease alone (cor pulmonale), COPD is the commonest cause: hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction and loss of the capillary bed raise pulmonary artery pressure. Pulmonary embolism gives acute right heart strain. Coronary artery disease and aortic stenosis act on the right side through the left heart failure they cause.
cardio-wb-cardio1-q10.why: Reasoned key. The source keyed COPD, but the most common cause of right-sided heart failure is left-sided heart failure, which was not among its options. Option E is added for the bank and keyed; COPD (cor pulmonale) is the commonest pulmonary cause.

options: Stenting is more effective than exercise training as a treatment for peripheral vascular disease

B and D are incorrect: physiologic hypertrophy first presents as eccentric hypertrophy, with sarcomeres added in series. C is incorrect: capillary density increases with training. E is correct: sarcomeres added in series increase the ventricle's volume capacity.

gi-wb-gi0-q112.answer:
TIPS shunts portal blood straight into the hepatic vein, so it raises right-heart preload and lets gut toxins bypass the liver.

  • A. Hepatic encephalopathy: diverting portal blood around the liver worsens it, so existing overt encephalopathy is a contraindication.
  • B. Severe pulmonary hypertension: the sudden rise in venous return can precipitate right heart failure; it is an absolute contraindication, along with congestive heart failure and severe tricuspid regurgitation.
  • D. Severe coagulopathy (e.g. INR above about 2.5) raises the risk of bleeding from the procedure.
  • C. Advanced cirrhosis is the setting TIPS is used in (refractory ascites, variceal bleeding). Very high MELD scores worsen the outcome, but cirrhosis itself is not a contraindication.
gi-wb-gi0-q112.why: Reasoned key. The source keyed A and D and called severe pulmonary hypertension only a risk. In the standard lists, severe pulmonary hypertension is an absolute contraindication to TIPS (with heart failure and severe tricuspid regurgitation), so B is keyed too. Advanced cirrhosis is the reason TIPS is done, not a contraindication in itself.

cardio-w3-meds2024-q1-1.answer: Most myocardial infarctions come from thrombosis on a previously atherosclerotic artery: a plaque ruptures or erodes and a thrombus forms on it. Partial atherosclerotic occlusion is also possible, but less common than thrombosis of an atherosclerotic coronary artery. Embolism into a coronary artery is rare.

cardio-w3-meds2024-q2-2.answer:
During the first 24 hours, cardiac enzymes rise in the blood as the membranes of dying heart cells begin to leak them (A), and cardiac myocytes lose their nuclei and undergo necrosis, seen microscopically (C).

Around day 2 to 3 neutrophils arrive, and macrophages follow to phagocytose debris (D). Fibroblasts then secrete collagen and build scar tissue (E), which is seen as white tissue macroscopically weeks later (B).

cardio-w3-meds2024-q3-3.answer: The coronary arteries run on the surface of the heart, so the cardiomyocytes closest to the surface receive blood first. When an artery is occluded, the muscle in the interior of the wall (the subendocardial zone) is the first to undergo necrosis, and the infarct then spreads outward toward the epicardium.
cardio-w3-meds2024-q3-3.why: The bank's answer to this question had slid onto the neighbouring question, so the key printed beside it belonged to another item. Keyed from the source's own explanation for this question, which is placed with it now.

cardio-w3-meds2024-q4-4.answer: Cardiac myocytes cannot divide, so ventricular hyperplasia does not occur; existing myocytes hypertrophy to generate the same contractility with fewer cells. Congestive heart failure follows when the ventricle cannot eject enough blood after the infarct, and the backup of blood into the venous system can congest the liver. Hemopericardium follows rupture of the heart wall and can cause tamponade. Arrhythmia is possible whenever damaged myocardium impairs impulse conduction.

cardio-w3-meds2024-q5-5.answer: The right coronary artery supplies the inferior wall in most people, so it is the artery most likely occluded in an inferior MI. The left anterior descending artery is occluded in anterior MIs, and the circumflex artery is often occluded in posterior and lateral MIs.

Troponin is measured, but it is not needed for the early diagnosis: it rises only several hours after the infarct begins, and treatment should not wait for it.

options: In a hospital without access to a catheterization lab, the patient should receive thrombolytic therapy with Tenecteplase administered intravenously.
In a hospital without access to a catheterization lab, the patient should receive Beta- Blockers and ACE-inhibitors administered orally.
In a hospital with access to a catheterization lab, the patient should receive thrombolytic therapy with Tenecteplase administered intravenously.
In a hospital with access to a catheterization lab, the patient should receive oral beta-blockers and wait for coronary angiography within 24 to 48 hours.
cardio-w3-meds2024-q9-9.answer: The ideal treatment for STEMI is primary percutaneous coronary intervention to establish reperfusion, but only a hospital with a catheterization lab can do it. Without one, the patient needs thrombolytic therapy (tenecteplase) to reperfuse. Beta-blockers and ACE inhibitors are used for their anti-ischemic effects but do not reperfuse. Delayed angiography within 24 to 48 hours is the NSTEMI approach; a STEMI with a cath lab available goes for primary PCI immediately.

Atrial fibrillation is an irregularly irregular narrow-complex rhythm with no discernible P waves, only a fine fibrillatory baseline: strip b.

Strip a has regular QRS complexes over a sawtooth baseline (atrial flutter). Strip c is a regular wide-complex tachycardia. Strip d is regular with P waves before each QRS.

cardio-w3-new-q4-4.stem: Arrange the evolution of the ECG in an unreperfused ST-elevation myocardial infarction in the correct order.
options: Normal, ST elevation, hyperacute T waves, Q waves, T inversion, persistent Q wave with normal ST-T
Normal, hyperacute T waves, Q waves, ST elevation, T inversion, persistent Q wave with normal ST-T
Normal, hyperacute T waves, ST elevation, Q waves, T inversion, persistent Q wave with normal ST-T
Normal, hyperacute T waves, ST elevation, T inversion, Q waves, normal ECG
Normal, T inversion, hyperacute T waves, ST elevation, Q waves, persistent Q wave with normal ST-T
cardio-w3-new-q4-4.answer:
From 04 - Myocardial Infarction. A STEMI that is not reperfused evolves through a fixed sequence (the source's key, A-E-F-B-D-C, traces it through the panels):

  • Normal baseline.
  • Hyperacute T waves: broad, peaked, asymmetric. These come first and precede ST elevation.
  • ST elevation: transmural injury in the ischemic zone.
  • Q waves develop as necrosis spreads from subendocardium to epicardium.
  • ST normalises, T inverts.
  • ST and T normal, Q wave persists for life.

A Q wave means necrosis, not ischemia, which is why it is the last thing to go and never does.
cardio-w3-new-q4-4.why: The bank's key was a sequence of panel letters, and the panels are unlabelled in the bank, so the letters could not be clicked or checked. The options now name the stages in words, keyed to the sequence the source's explanation traces.

cardio-wb-cardio1-q1.answer: ACE inhibitors cause hyperkalemia, not hypokalemia: less angiotensin II means less aldosterone, so the kidney excretes less potassium. The other statements are true. Cough comes from bradykinin, which ACE normally breaks down. ACE inhibitors protect the kidney by dilating the efferent arteriole and lowering intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria. Lower angiotensin II also damps sympathetic outflow and noradrenaline release.

cardio-wb-cardio1-q2.answer:
A prior heart attack is a common cause of secondary (ischemic) mitral regurgitation: infarction of the papillary muscle or the wall beneath it, and remodelling of the left ventricle, pull the leaflets apart so they no longer meet.

Rheumatic heart disease can cause regurgitation, but its signature mitral lesion is stenosis (fused commissures). Hypertension and smoking alone, obesity and diabetes, and congenital heart disease in general are not specific causes of mitral regurgitation.
cardio-wb-cardio1-q2.why: The workbook's answer for this question was lost: the text printed with it belongs to a different item (the 6 P's of peripheral vascular disease). Keyed from the lecture teaching; the explanation is written for the bank. Rheumatic heart disease most classically gives mitral stenosis, so the patient with prior MI and angina (ischemic, secondary mitral regurgitation) is keyed.

cardio-wb-cardio1-q3.answer: Surgery for aortic regurgitation is indicated for severe AR with symptoms, or with left ventricular dysfunction or significant LV dilation even without symptoms. The asymptomatic patient with mild to moderate AR and stable echocardiograms meets none of these, so she is followed with serial echo. The symptomatic patient with severe AR (A) and the asymptomatic patient with a failing, dilated LV (D) both need surgery; C is closer to the threshold than B.

cardio-wb-cardio1-q5.answer: Constrictive pericarditis follows anything that inflames and then scars the pericardium. The common causes are idiopathic or viral pericarditis, prior cardiac surgery and mediastinal radiation in high-income countries, and tuberculosis worldwide. Mitral valve prolapse is a valve disease and does not involve the pericardium.

ent-w9-new-q1-1.stem:
A patient comes in with pain and swelling in their right submandibular gland and it gets worse when eating. Which of the following are possible complications of their condition?

  1. Necrosis
  2. Acute suppurative sialadenitis
  3. Ductal stricture
  4. Abscess
  5. Fistula
ent-w9-new-q1-1.answer: From 04 - Adult Head & Neck Masses. Pain and submandibular swelling that worsen with eating are salivary colic from sialolithiasis, and the submandibular gland is the most common site. The stone causes stasis, and its complications follow from obstruction and infection: acute suppurative sialadenitis (II), ductal stricture (III), abscess when the sialadenitis progresses (IV), and fistula, the gland draining through the skin (V). Necrosis (I) is not a listed complication.
ent-w9-new-q1-1.why: Reasoned key. The source printed D (I, II, V), but its own explanation, and the sialolithiasis and acute sialadenitis notes, list sialadenitis, ductal stricture, abscess and fistula and never necrosis: that is C (II, III, IV, V).

ent-w9-new-q9-9.stem:
Regarding thyroid nodules, which of the following presentations are concerning for malignant masses?

  1. First degree relative with thyroid cancer
  2. Age <20 or >70
  3. Family history of autoimmune disorders
  4. Nodules immobile with swallowing
  5. Pain
  6. Smoking
ent-w9-new-q9-9.answer: A first degree relative with thyroid cancer (I), age under 20 or over 70 (II) and a nodule fixed to surrounding structures so it does not move with swallowing (IV) are concerning for malignancy. A family history of autoimmune disease (III) and pain (V) point to benign thyroid disease such as thyroiditis or a bleed into a cyst. Smoking (VI) is not a risk factor for thyroid cancer specifically.

gi-w12-meds2024-q11-11.stem: Which of the following treatments should be considered for a patient who has overdosed on acetaminophen?
gi-w12-meds2024-q11-11.answer: N-acetylcysteine should be considered for patients who overdosed on acetaminophen (Tylenol), using the 200 line nomogram. It replenishes glutathione so the toxic metabolite NAPQI is detoxified. Corticosteroids are used for severe alcoholic hepatitis, tenofovir treats hepatitis B, lactulose treats hepatic encephalopathy, and ursodeoxycholic acid treats primary biliary cholangitis.
